At the edge of the grocery store parking lot, a pear tree grows through a break in the asphalt. Nobody planted it there on purpose. Its trunk leans away from the loading dock, and each spring it flowers above the carts and painted arrows.

In August, the pears are hard and small. Most fall before they ripen. A few people pick them anyway, pressing a thumb against the skin, hoping for some give. Once, I saw a woman take three and put them carefully in her handbag. She looked up through the branches for a fourth, then changed her mind.

The store has repaved the lot twice. Each time, the new blacktop stops at the same uneven circle of old pavement around the trunk. Perhaps removing the tree would cost more than leaving it. Whatever the reason, there is still a place to stand in its shade while you look for your keys.
